claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a duplex FCC/BCC microstructure with relatively coarse interfaces and low phase-boundary density.
Controlled rapid solidification followed by sub-transus annealing can increase FCC/BCC phase-boundary density by tailoring phase fractions and distributions.
The engineered FCC/BCC boundary network will remain stable under the proposed service conditions.
Increasing FCC/BCC phase-boundary density creates more obstacles to dislocation motion.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as pinning sites for dislocation glide.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as pinning sites for dislocation climb.
Inhibiting dislocation movement at phase boundaries reduces dislocation accumulation.
Reduced dislocation accumulation lowers the steady-state creep rate.
A coating with high FCC/BCC interface density will have a significantly lower creep rate than the lower-density baseline coating.
A coating with high FCC/BCC interface density will deform more uniformly than the baseline coating.
FCC/BCC interfaces can mediate dislocation transfer and annihilation and thereby mitigate early strain localization.
The proposed creep-resistance mechanism applies while the duplex microstructure remains phase-stable under sustained loading.
Excessively high temperatures may coarsen or destabilize interfaces.
Coarsening or destabilization of interfaces at high temperature would undermine the proposed creep-resistance benefit.
The processing used to increase interface density may also alter other microstructural features relevant to protective performance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction, or failure to observe interface pinning, would falsify the hypothesis.
